questions.question: What does `typeof null` return, and why is this notable?
options: "object" — a long-standing historical quirk of the language, kept for backward compatibility
"undefined" — because null represents absence of a value
questions.explanation: typeof null returning "object" is a famous bug from the original JS implementation that has remained for compatibility ever since.

questions.question: Why does `obj2.count = 20` also change `obj1.count` after `const obj2 = obj1`?
options: const prevents reassignment but objects are assigned by reference, so obj1 and obj2 point to the same underlying object
JavaScript automatically synchronizes variables with the same shape
This only happens in non-strict mode
It doesn't — this is a trick question, obj1.count stays 10
questions.explanation: Objects are reference types: both variables hold a reference to the same object in memory, so mutating it via either variable is visible through both.

questions.question: Why does `"0" == false` evaluate to true?
options: Because loose equality coerces both operands toward a common type — here, "0" becomes the number 0, and false also becomes 0
Because strings and booleans are the same type internally
This is actually false, not true
questions.explanation: == applies a coercion algorithm when operand types differ; both "0" and false ultimately compare as the number 0.

questions.question: What is the reliable way to check whether a value is NaN?
questions.explanation: NaN is never equal to anything, including itself, so equality checks always fail; Number.isNaN is the dedicated, coercion-free check.
